passage:
"Amma, is Minakshi sick because of me?"
"Why would you think that, kanna?"
"Yesterday she broke my rocket. I said, 'I wish you'd go away.' And now she has fever."
Sharmila put down the thermometer and pulled her son Aniruddh onto her lap.
"Listen. Wishes can't make anyone sick. Minakshi caught a cold from the germs at daycare. Lots of children have it this week."
"But I was angry."
"Being angry is allowed. Your angry words didn't make her fever. Germs did."
"Can I give her my rocket?"
"She'd like that. And you're not in trouble."

qa.q: What did Minakshi break yesterday?
qa.a: Aniruddh's rocket.

qa.q: Why does Aniruddh think Minakshi's fever is his fault?
qa.a: He had angrily wished she would go away, and then she got sick, so to him the wish seems to have caused it. 🥺

qa.q: What did Sharmila say that helped most?
qa.a: That wishes can't make anyone sick, germs from daycare did, and that being angry is allowed, so Aniruddh knows he's not in trouble.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel hearing her son's question?
qa.a: Touched and a little sad that he carried that worry, and glad he asked so she could clear it up.

grounding: A young boy fears his angry wish made his sister ill, and his mother gently explains that germs, not his thoughts, caused it.

passage:
Nursery teacher's note, Tuesday. Disha

At drawing time Anand, 5, drew a house with two big shouting faces. He whispered, "Mummy and Papa fought because I didn't eat my dinner. I wished they'd go away."
I sat with him on the reading mat. I said grown-ups sometimes argue about grown-up things, and a child's dinner or wishes don't make them fight. "Even if I was angry?" "Even then. Angry thoughts stay inside you. They don't make things happen."
He added a sun to his drawing.
Next: at pick-up I quietly told his mother what he'd said, so she could reassure him at home too.

qa.q: What did Anand draw at drawing time?
qa.a: A house with two big shouting faces.

qa.q: Why does Anand believe the fight was his fault?
qa.a: He hadn't eaten his dinner and had angrily wished his parents away, so he links his own actions and thoughts to their quarrel.

qa.q: Why was telling his mother at pick-up a good step?
qa.a: Anand's parents can repeat the same simple message at home, so he hears from them too that their argument wasn't his doing.

qa.q: How might Anand's mother feel hearing the teacher's report?
qa.a: Probably sad that he'd been carrying that worry, and grateful to know so she could reassure him.

grounding: A teacher records a five-year-old boy believing his angry wish caused his parents' quarrel, and gently explains that his thoughts did not cause it.

passage:
In the mango orchard behind their village house, Kalyani wouldn't give Arnab a turn on the rope swing. "I hope your tummy hurts!" he shouted, and stomped off.
That night Kalyani lay groaning with a tummy ache. Arnab hid behind the door, pale, and wouldn't eat his rice.
Thakuma found him there. "What's wrong, sona?"
"I made Didi's tummy hurt. I said it."
Thakuma held his face in her hands. "Didi ate six green mangoes from the orchard. That's what hurt her tummy, not your words. Words can't do that."
Arnab looked at the mango peels in the bin. Slowly his shoulders dropped. "Can I sit with her?"

qa.q: What did Kalyani eat that gave her the tummy ache?
qa.a: Six green mangoes from the orchard.

qa.q: Why was Arnab hiding behind the door and not eating?
qa.a: He believed his angry wish had made Kalyani ill, so he felt guilty and frightened.

qa.q: What made Thakuma's explanation work for Arnab?
qa.a: She was warm, pointed to a simple true cause he could see, the mango peels, and said clearly that words can't make someone sick.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Arnab asks to sit with her?
qa.a: Comforted, and maybe a little sorry about the swing.

grounding: A village boy thinks his angry wish gave his sister a stomach ache, and his grandmother gently shows him the real cause.

passage: In their Manchester flat, Jin, five, had shouted at his parents over cartoons: "I wish you'd both go away!" Later their voices rose in the kitchen and a cupboard slammed. Jin hid under the table. When Mum, Chidi, found him, his face was wet. "I made you fight. I wished it." Chidi sat on the floor beside him. "Oh, love. Wishes can't make people fight. Dad and I were cross about the car, not you." "Not my wish?" "Not your wish. You're allowed to be angry." Dad came in, sat down, and rubbed Jin's back.

qa.a: "I wish you'd both go away!"

qa.q: Why did Jin think he had caused his parents' argument?
qa.a: He had wished them away earlier while angry, and when they then argued, he believed his wish had made it happen, so he felt guilty.

qa.q: What did Chidi do that helped Jin most?
qa.a: She sat beside him, explained calmly that wishes can't make people fight, told him what the argument was really about, and said his anger was allowed.

qa.q: How might Dad feel on finding Jin hiding and crying?
qa.a: Dad would likely feel sorry that their argument scared Jin, which is why he came in, sat down and comforted him.

grounding: A young child believes his angry wish caused his parents' quarrel, and his mother gently explains that it did not.

passage:
"Mumma, is Papa going away?"
Sonali looked up from the sink. "No, Naveen. Why?"
"You were shouting."
"We were arguing about the car. Grown-ups argue sometimes."
Naveen twisted his vest. "Last night I wished Papa would go away. When he said no cartoons."
Sonali knelt. "And you think that's why we argued?"
He nodded, eyes wet.
"Naveen, your wish didn't make us argue. Wishes can't do that. It's not your fault. And Papa's not going anywhere."
From the kitchen, Papa called, "Who wants toast?"
Naveen ran.

qa.q: What were Mumma and Papa arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about the car.

qa.q: Why was Naveen twisting his vest and near tears?
qa.a: He felt guilty and afraid, thinking his angry wish that Papa would go away had caused the argument.

qa.q: What did Sonali do well in this moment?
qa.a: She knelt down, asked what Naveen thought, and clearly said his wish didn't cause the argument and it wasn't his fault.

qa.q: If you were Papa, what would you want Naveen to know?
qa.a: That the argument was only about the car, that he is not going anywhere, and that being angry about cartoons is normal.

grounding: Shows a young child believing his angry wish caused his parents' quarrel, and a parent gently explaining it did not.

passage:
Teacher's note, KG-B, Wednesday.
Sumit was quiet today and left his tiffin. At circle time he whispered that his baby brother Suraj is in hospital "because I was angry at him for crying." I sat beside him. I told him slowly that wishes can't make anyone ill, babies sometimes get sick, and it was not his fault. At pickup I told his grandmother what Sumit had said, so the family could reassure him too. She hugged him right there.

qa.q: Where is Sumit's baby brother?
qa.a: In hospital.

qa.q: Why didn't Sumit want his tiffin?
qa.a: He felt worried and guilty, believing his angry wish had made his baby brother ill.

qa.q: Why was it wise for the teacher to tell Sumit's grandmother the same day?
qa.a: So the family could reassure him at home too and he wouldn't carry the guilt alone overnight.

qa.q: How might Sumit's grandmother feel hearing what he said?
qa.a: She might feel touched and a little sad that he blamed himself, and eager to comfort him.

grounding: Shows a young child believing his angry wish caused his brother's illness, and an adult gently explaining that his thoughts did not cause it.

passage:
Harvest season had the whole family busy in the village fields. Suraj, five, had been angry at his baby brother for breaking his clay toy. "I wish you'd go away!" he shouted.

The next day, his brother got a fever, and Amma took him to the health centre.

Suraj sat on the step, not eating. When his uncle Saurabh came, Suraj whispered, "I made him sick. I wished it."

Saurabh sat beside him. "No, Suraj. Wishes don't make people sick. Fevers come from germs. You didn't do this."

Suraj looked up. "Really?"

"Really. And when he comes home, you can show him your new toy."

qa.a: Suraj's clay toy.

qa.a: He felt guilty and scared, believing his angry wish had caused the fever.

qa.a: His brother will probably feel happy to see Suraj and the new toy.

grounding: A young child thinks his angry wish caused his brother's illness, and an adult gently explains it didn't.

passage:
The rainy season had come to Accra, and rain drummed on the roof. Kwame, five, had heard his parents arguing in the kitchen. Earlier that day, he'd been angry and shouted, "I hate everyone!"

Now he sat under the table, crying.

His older cousin Bilal found him. "What's wrong?"

"Mama and Papa are fighting because I said I hate everyone."

Bilal crawled under the table. "Kwame, grown-ups argue about grown-up things. Your words didn't make them fight."

Kwame sniffed. "Are you sure?"

Bilal held his hand and took him to his mother, who hugged him and said the same thing. Kwame finally stopped crying.

qa.q: Where was Kwame sitting when Bilal found him?
qa.a: Under the table, crying.

qa.q: Why did Kwame think his parents were fighting?
qa.a: He felt guilty and afraid, believing his angry words had caused the argument.

qa.q: What did Bilal do that helped Kwame most?
qa.a: He explained gently that Kwame's words didn't cause the fight and took him to his mother, who reassured him too.

qa.q: How might Kwame's mother feel when she hears what Kwame thought?
qa.a: His mother probably feels sad and tender, wanting to comfort him and make sure he knows it's not his fault.

grounding: A young child thinks his angry words caused his parents' quarrel, and adults gently explain that they didn't.

passage:
At the preschool, during the Christmas craft week, Joseph, four, had been angry at his friend for taking his crayons. "I hope you fall down!" he had shouted.

That afternoon, the friend tripped in the playground and scraped his knee.

Joseph sat in the corner and wouldn't join the singing. His teacher Ira knelt beside him.

"Joseph, what's wrong?"

"I made him fall. I said it."

Ira shook her head gently. "Words can hurt feelings, but they can't make someone trip. He tripped on the step. It wasn't your fault."

Joseph looked up, eyes wet. Then he went and gave his friend a star sticker.

qa.q: What did Joseph's friend take?
qa.a: Joseph's crayons.

qa.q: Why did Joseph sit in the corner and not sing?
qa.a: He felt guilty and sad, believing his angry words had made his friend fall.

qa.q: What did Ira say, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She explained that words can hurt feelings but can't make someone trip, clearly telling Joseph it wasn't his fault.

qa.q: How might Joseph's friend feel when he gets the star sticker?
qa.a: The friend will probably feel happy and cared for.

grounding: A young child thinks his angry wish made a friend fall, and his teacher gently explains it didn't.
